definition: Merriam-Webster's Word of the Day for November 2, 2026 is: satiate &#149; \SAY-shee-ayt\&nbsp; &#149; verb To satiate a need, desire, etc., is to satisfy it fully. // The new restaurant’s menu promises to satiate diners’ cravings for comfort food, offering fresh spins on classic, time-honored fare. The time has come at last to share the “sad” history of satiate , by which we mean that the two words— sad and satiate —are etymologically connected, not that the details will have you reaching for the tissue box. Both satiate and sad are related to the Latin satis , meaning “enough.” When we say our desire, thirst, curiosity, etc. has been satiated, we mean it has been fully satisfied ( satisfy being another satis descendant)—in other words, we’ve had enough. Satiate and sate (believed to be an alteration and shortening of satiate ) sometimes imply simple contentment, but often suggest that having enough has dulled interest or desire for more, as in “Years of globe-trotting satiated their interest in travel.”
